facts.text: A scanned PDF is created from paper documents run through an optical scanner; an electronically converted PDF is created from a word processor and is text searchable.
Scanned PDFs are typically just images of pages; unless OCR is applied, screen readers and other assistive technology cannot interpret the content.
A quick test: search for a word you can see (Ctrl+F); if it gets highlighted, the PDF has real text rather than being a scanned image of text.
If a PDF is not text-searchable, you cannot copy its text.
OCR (optical character recognition) converts images of typed, handwritten or printed text into machine-encoded text, e.g. from a scanned document or a photo of a document.
Even OCR'd scanned PDFs usually place the text layer under the page image, so zooming shows pixelation and the hidden text can be inaccurate.
PDF/A is an ISO-standardized (ISO 19005) version of PDF specialized for archiving and long-term preservation.
Microsoft Office can export ISO 19005-1 (PDF/A) compliant files.

statistics.context: PDF was first released June 15, 1993 and is now standardized as ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0).

Lossy pattern-matching compression (JBIG2) in some photocopiers has substituted digits such as "6" and "8".
Copiers and printers can be traced by imperfections in output; mechanical tolerances in toner and paper feed cause banding.
OCR pre-processing includes de-skewing, despeckling and binarization — the inverse of the skew, speckle and threshold effects of real scans.
NARA's QA checklist lists clipping, misregistration, quantization errors, skew and improper cropping as scan defects.
